title: ChatGPT’s Computer History tracks your clicks and keystrokes
summary: ChatGPT's desktop app on macOS has a new feature called Computer History that turns your actions into training data, learning how you work, suggesting automations, and even picking up tasks you left half done. It uses your activity to build a timeline that ChatGPT and Codex can…
whatHappening: OpenAI has introduced Computer History, a new feature in ChatGPT's macOS desktop app that monitors user clicks and keystrokes to build an activity timeline. The system uses this behavioral data to train AI models, suggest automations, and resume incomplete tasks.
whoInvolved: OpenAI, the San Francisco-based AI research organization that developed ChatGPT, is rolling out this feature. ChatGPT, which launched in November 2022 and catalyzed the current AI boom, is the flagship product receiving this capability through its desktop application.
whyMatters: This feature represents a significant expansion in how AI systems collect and utilize personal user data, moving beyond text inputs to comprehensive activity monitoring. The implications touch on privacy concerns, data governance, and the methods by which AI models are trained on real-world human behavior at scale.
articleBody:
OpenAI has introduced a new tracking feature called Computer History to ChatGPT's macOS desktop application that transforms user activity into machine learning fuel. The feature monitors clicks and keystrokes, converting them into a timeline that ChatGPT and Codex can access to learn user patterns, according to The Verge. The system doesn't merely record actions—it actively uses them to suggest automations and even identify and complete tasks users have abandoned mid-workflow.

The Computer History feature represents a departure from traditional AI training methodologies. While ChatGPT, which launched in November 2022 and sparked the current wave of generative AI investment, originally trained on text-based datasets, Computer History extends this to direct behavioral monitoring of individual users. This granular activity tracking transforms desktop interaction into granular training data, allowing the AI system to build sophisticated models of how specific users work.

The feature's capability to suggest automations and complete unfinished tasks highlights its practical utility. Rather than simply recording what users do, the system analyzes patterns in that activity to infer intent and automate repetitive workflows. This positions ChatGPT's desktop experience as something closer to an active agent in a user's workflow rather than a passive tool awaiting prompts.

The introduction of Computer History occurs as OpenAI continues expanding ChatGPT beyond its original freemium conversational interface. OpenAI operates ChatGPT on a freemium model, making the service accessible to broad audiences while monetizing through premium tiers and enterprise offerings. The macOS desktop application itself represents expansion beyond the web-based interface, and Computer History marks an evolution in how the platform engages with user environments.

The feature raises immediate questions about data collection scope and retention. Users' keystroke and click patterns constitute highly sensitive behavioral data—information that has traditionally been the domain of operating systems and applications with explicit user awareness. By integrating this collection directly into ChatGPT, OpenAI is positioning AI training on personal activity as a standard feature of consumer software.

title: Polaroid’s tiny instant camera is $72 and includes a free pack of film
summary: The compact Polaroid Go is great for road trips and adventures. | Image: Polaroid Smartphone cameras are convenient, but they lack the charm of analog instant cameras. If you’re trying to relive the nostalgia of waiting for an instant photo to develop, Amazon is selling the…
whatHappening: Polaroid is offering its compact Go instant camera for $72 with a free pack of film included, making analog instant photography more accessible. The tiny camera targets consumers seeking the tactile nostalgia of physical instant prints rather than smartphone photos.
whoInvolved: Polaroid Corporation, the American company that pioneered consumer instant cameras and film starting in the mid-20th century, is behind the Go model. The deal is currently available through Amazon.
whyMatters: The aggressive pricing signals renewed interest in instant analog cameras as a counter to digital photography's dominance. For consumers fatigued by screens and seeking tangible, shareable moments—especially during travel—affordable instant options lower the barrier to entry for a format that had largely faded from mainstream consumer use.
articleBody:
Amazon is currently selling Polaroid's Go instant camera at $72, bundled with a complimentary pack of film—a significant discount that makes the device an accessible entry point for consumers curious about analog instant photography. The tiny, pocket-sized camera is marketed as ideal for road trips and outdoor adventures, positioning it as a tool for capturing and sharing physical memories in an age dominated by smartphone cameras.

Instant cameras, which use self-developing film to produce a chemically developed print within minutes of the shot, represent a niche that was largely abandoned by mainstream manufacturers over the past two decades. Polaroid Corporation pioneered this category, transforming instant photography into a consumer staple in the 1970s and 1980s. Though the company eventually exited the instant film market, the Polaroid brand and intellectual property are now owned and operated by Polaroid B.V., a Dutch manufacturer that has revived the brand with new camera models and film stocks in recent years.

Smartphone cameras, despite their convenience and technical sophistication, lack the tactile and temporal experience that instant film provides. The physical act of waiting for an image to slowly develop, combined with the one-shot permanence of instant film, creates a fundamentally different relationship with photography—one that many younger consumers now find appealing as a counterpoint to the infinite, disposable nature of digital images. According to The Verge, the Go camera's compact form factor and throwback aesthetic make it particularly suited for travel and casual use where a dedicated camera might otherwise feel cumbersome.

The $72 price point, especially with included film, removes a historical friction point in the instant camera market: the high upfront cost of both the camera and its consumable film stock. Polaroid film has traditionally been expensive, with individual packs running $15 or more, making the hobby prohibitively costly for casual users. By bundling film with the hardware at a competitive total price, this offer acknowledges that the real barrier to adoption was not nostalgia alone but practical affordability.

The revival of instant cameras reflects a broader cultural pattern of seeking analog alternatives to digital tools—from vinyl records to printed books—but Polaroid's specific bet here is on the Go's portability and the social utility of physical prints in an era of shareable, shareable moments. Whether this represents a sustained resurgence or a niche indulgence remains to be seen, but the company's willingness to aggressively price its entry-level model suggests confidence in renewed consumer demand.

title: Have a laugh at AI’s expense by roleplaying as a chatbot
summary: If you squint you can just about make out the hat. | Screenshot: Terrence O’Brien / The Verge Your AI Slop Bores Me is brilliant in its simplicity. There are two tabs: human and LARP as an AI. On one side you enter a request. On the other, you submit an answer. But the important…
whatHappening: A new website called "Your AI Slop Bores Me" lets people mock artificial intelligence by roleplaying as chatbots themselves. The site presents a humorous contrast between human requests and deliberately awkward AI-style responses, inviting users to laugh at AI's characteristic quirks and stilted phrasing.
whoInvolved: The Verge is reporting on the website, which appears to be a creative project by an independent developer or small team poking fun at generative AI systems. No major companies are directly involved in creating the tool, though it's a commentary on the broader AI industry.
whyMatters: The site reflects growing fatigue with AI-generated content and the recognizable patterns of chatbot speech that now pervade the internet. As AI tools become ubiquitous, cultural pushback through humor and parody serves as a barometer for public sentiment about AI's limitations and overuse.
articleBody:
A clever new website is giving internet users a chance to mock artificial intelligence by becoming the thing they mock. "Your AI Slop Bores Me" strips away the veneer of technological sophistication and invites people to experience the humor in how chatbots actually communicate. The site's premise is elegantly straightforward: two tabs sit side by side, one labeled "human" and the other "LARP as an AI." Users enter a prompt on the human side, then attempt to respond as a chatbot would on the other.

The brilliance lies in its simplicity, according to The Verge. Rather than explaining what makes AI responses feel hollow or repetitive, the site lets users discover it themselves through direct participation. By role-playing as a chatbot, players internalize the patterns—the hedging language, the apologetic qualifiers, the tendency to restate obvious points—that have become instantly recognizable markers of generative AI output. The result is both comedic and revealing about what has become known colloquially as "AI slop," the term now used to describe low-effort, formulaic content churned out by language models.

The emergence of projects like this reflects a cultural moment where AI enthusiasm has begun to curdle into skepticism and fatigue. For much of 2023 and 2024, generative AI tools captured widespread fascination and venture capital enthusiasm. But as these systems became integrated into more products and services, their limitations became increasingly apparent—and increasingly annoying. The sameness of AI-generated text, the confident spouting of half-truths, and the way chatbots hedge every statement with disclaimers have become sources of genuine frustration for users.

Satire and parody have long served as cultural pressure valves, allowing people to process and critique phenomena that feel overwhelming or inescapable. "Your AI Slop Bores Me" operates in this tradition, transforming critique into play. Rather than reading a thinkpiece about why AI language is annoying, users can spend five minutes actively generating their own terrible AI responses and laugh at how easy it is. The act of participation makes the critique sharper and more memorable.

The site also taps into a broader conversation about authenticity and originality in an age of algorithmic content. As AI systems proliferate, the ability to distinguish human from machine-generated work becomes both more important and more difficult. Projects that highlight the distinctive markers of AI output serve a practical purpose beyond entertainment—they train human perception to notice patterns and quirks that might otherwise go unexamined.

title: Matt Groening lets slip that Simpsons: Hit & Run might be making a comeback
summary: Doh! | Image: Activision / 20th Century Fox At D23, when asked about the potential for a sequel to the cult classic The Simpsons: Hit & Run game, Matt Groening replied, "I think the original game is coming back in some form," before current showrunner Matt Selman added, "or…
whatHappening: Matt Groening has hinted at D23 that The Simpsons: Hit & Run, the cult classic 2003 video game, is being revived in some form. The announcement comes two decades after the original game's release, sparking speculation about whether a sequel or remaster is in the works.
whoInvolved: Matt Groening is the creator of The Simpsons television series and has been a driving force behind the franchise's expansion into gaming and other media. Matt Selman, the current showrunner of The Simpsons, was also present at D23 and weighed in on the potential revival.
whyMatters: A revival of Hit & Run could signal renewed interest in legacy gaming properties tied to major entertainment franchises, particularly as studios look to capitalize on nostalgia. For The Simpsons franchise, re-entering the gaming space after years of dormancy represents a potential new revenue stream and way to engage fans across platforms.
articleBody:
At D23, the annual fan convention celebrating Disney's creative output, Matt Groening shared unexpected news about a potential return for The Simpsons: Hit & Run. When asked directly about the possibility of a sequel to the beloved driving game, Groening responded with optimism, stating that "the original game is coming back in some form." Current Simpsons showrunner Matt Selman was on hand and appeared to hint at further developments, though details remain sparse.

The Simpsons: Hit & Run was originally developed by Radical Entertainment and published by Vivendi Universal Games in 2003. The action-adventure game became a cult classic among players, featuring driving and exploration mechanics set in the iconic town of Springfield. As the 22nd installment in The Simpsons series of video games, it occupied a unique position in the franchise's gaming history, blending the show's trademark humor with open-world gameplay that appealed to both devoted fans and casual gamers.

According to The Verge, the hints dropped at D23 have reignited speculation about what form this revival might take. Groening's phrasing—"coming back in some form"—leaves room for multiple interpretations, from a straight remaster of the original game to a full sequel or even a different type of release entirely. Selman's cryptic addition to the conversation suggested that official announcements may be forthcoming, though neither executive provided concrete details or timelines.

The potential return of Hit & Run comes at a time when video game publishers and entertainment companies are increasingly mining their back catalogs for IP with established fan bases. Classic games tied to major franchises have proven commercially viable through remasters and re-releases, particularly when nostalgia-driven marketing targets players who grew up with the original titles. For The Simpsons, which remains one of the most enduring animated series in television history, gaming represents a natural avenue for franchise extension.

The original Hit & Run earned its cult status through faithful adaptation of the show's world and humor, allowing players to inhabit Springfield and interact with familiar characters and locations. A return to the franchise could similarly capitalize on the show's 35-year run and the deep affection fans hold for its classic era. Whether the revival focuses on updating the original experience for modern gaming systems or launching an entirely new game remains to be seen.

title: Switched on Pop’s Nate Sloan and Charlie Harding love fresh vegetables and guitar pedals
summary: They’re the Lennon–McCartney of overanalyzing pop music. | Image: Daniel Randall As if you needed more reason to love Carly Rae Jepsen's "Call Me Maybe" beyond its pop perfection, it is also, according to lore, the genesis for Switched on Pop, one of the best music podcasts out…
whatHappening: Nate Sloan and Charlie Harding, hosts of the acclaimed music podcast Switched on Pop, are profiled by The Verge in a feature that explores their personalities and interests beyond their deep dives into pop music analysis.
whoInvolved: Nate Sloan is a musicologist and Charlie Harding is a songwriter; together they created Switched on Pop in 2014, a podcast dedicated to analyzing popular music that has become recognized as one of the best music podcasts available.
whyMatters: The profile offers insight into the creative minds behind one of contemporary music criticism's most influential platforms, humanizing the analytical voices that have shaped how millions of listeners understand pop music. Their documented interests—from fresh vegetables to guitar pedals—reveal the eclectic range of influences that inform their approach to musical criticism.
articleBody:
Nate Sloan and Charlie Harding have built a reputation as the Lennon–McCartney of pop music analysis through their podcast Switched on Pop, which launched in 2014. According to The Verge, the duo brings an unusually deep analytical lens to contemporary hits, breaking down production, harmony, and cultural resonance in ways that have resonated with music fans seeking substance alongside streaming playlists.

The podcast's origin story traces back to Carly Rae Jepsen's "Call Me Maybe," which according to lore served as the genesis for the show. Sloan, a musicologist, and Harding, a songwriter, found in that deceptively simple earworm a perfect case study for what makes pop music tick. Rather than dismiss the track as frivolous, they recognized its architectural sophistication and cultural moment, setting the tone for the show's entire approach: taking pop seriously as a legitimate subject for rigorous analysis.

Beyond their podcast work, the profile reveals Sloan and Harding to be thoughtful individuals with surprisingly varied interests. Their passion for fresh vegetables and guitar pedals suggests a curiosity that extends well beyond music theory and production techniques. These seemingly disparate interests—horticultural freshness and sonic equipment—hint at a shared sensibility: a drive to understand how things work, whether in a kitchen, a studio, or on a record.

Since its 2014 debut, Switched on Pop has become a cultural touchstone for music criticism in the streaming era. The show's success lies partly in Sloan and Harding's genuine enthusiasm for their subject matter, refusing the pretension that often accompanies music analysis while maintaining intellectual rigor. They treat pop music not as a guilty pleasure or a commercial product to be disdained, but as worthy of the same close attention classical musicians and serious critics have long reserved for other genres.

The Verge's profile underscores how Sloan and Harding have helped legitimize pop music criticism during an era when streaming algorithms and social media have fragmented listening habits. Their work demonstrates that pop analysis need not be either condescending toward its subject or entirely uncritical in its approach. Instead, by combining Sloan's musicological training with Harding's insider knowledge of songwriting, they've created a framework for understanding contemporary music that appeals to casual listeners and music professionals alike.

title: A RAMageddon guide to back-to-school laptop shopping
summary: The MacBook Neo is an easy recommendation. | Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge If you’re a student looking for an affordable laptop, I have bad news and I have good news. The bad news is that computer prices are out of whack due to the ongoing RAM and storage crunch,…
whatHappening: Computer prices have become inflated due to ongoing RAM and storage shortages, making back-to-school laptop shopping challenging for budget-conscious students. The Verge is offering guidance on navigating the market, with the MacBook Neo highlighted as an accessible recommendation despite broader pricing pressures.
whoInvolved: Apple, the computer manufacturer behind the MacBook line, is central to this story. The MacBook brand has been Apple's primary laptop offering since 2006, with the newer MacBook Neo entering the lineup in 2026 as part of the company's efforts to serve different market segments.
whyMatters: High laptop prices during back-to-school season directly affect students' ability to purchase necessary computing equipment for their studies. The RAM and storage crunch creating these inflated prices has broader implications for the entire consumer electronics market, potentially influencing purchasing decisions across educational institutions and households.
articleBody:
Back-to-school season traditionally brings a surge in laptop purchases, but this year students and parents face an unusually difficult market. Computer prices have become significantly elevated due to ongoing shortages in RAM and storage components, creating what amounts to a supply-driven pricing crisis. The Verge reports that finding an affordable laptop requires careful shopping and realistic expectations about what features students can secure at reasonable price points.

Apple's laptop offerings have long dominated the education market. The MacBook brand, which replaced the PowerBook and iBook lines during Apple's transition to Intel processors in 2006, currently consists of the MacBook Pro, MacBook Air, and the newer MacBook Neo. These machines run macOS and serve different price tiers and user needs. According to The Verge, the MacBook Neo represents an easy recommendation for students seeking affordability, suggesting that Apple has positioned this newer entry-level model as a practical option even as component costs remain elevated.

The supply chain disruptions affecting RAM and storage components stem from broader semiconductor market dynamics. Random-access memory, which serves as the working storage for computer operations, has become particularly constrained. These components are fundamental to laptop functionality, storing both data and machine code that applications require during operation. When RAM and storage supplies tighten, manufacturers have limited ability to reduce prices, pushing costs to consumers.

For students shopping this season, the guidance appears to be twofold: accept that prices are higher than historical norms, but recognize that some options remain more reasonable than others. The MacBook Neo's emergence as a recommended choice suggests Apple has created a product specifically designed to address budget constraints during this period of elevated component costs. Students evaluating laptops should prioritize their actual needs rather than aspirational specifications, given that premium configurations will command premium prices in this constrained market.

title: Lamborghini’s flagship Revuelto levels up with SV trim
summary: A lot of automakers talk about wanting to minimize or eliminate driver distractions so as to make the experience of driving more rewarding and safer overall. Lamborghini has a different strategy; it wants the driver to become one with their vehicle. This helps explain the…
whatHappening: Lamborghini has unveiled a new SV trim for its flagship Revuelto hybrid supercar, elevating the model with enhanced performance and features. The move represents the Italian automaker's latest iteration of its successor to the legendary Aventador.
whoInvolved: Lamborghini, the Italian luxury sports car manufacturer based in Sant'Agata Bolognese and owned by the Volkswagen Group through Audi, is introducing this new variant. The Revuelto itself debuted in March 2023 as a mid-engine plug-in hybrid sports car replacing the Aventador.
whyMatters: The SV trim signals Lamborghini's continued commitment to pushing the Revuelto platform toward higher performance and driver engagement, a key strategy for differentiating premium supercars in an increasingly regulated automotive market. As electrification becomes mandatory across the industry, how flagship models like the Revuelto evolve will influence luxury carmakers' approach to balancing power, efficiency, and the visceral driving experience.
articleBody:
Lamborghini has leveled up its flagship Revuelto with a new SV trim, continuing to develop the mid-engine hybrid supercar that launched in March 2023 as the successor to the iconic Aventador. According to The Verge, the automaker is taking a distinctive approach to vehicle design, one that prioritizes driver immersion rather than distraction reduction—a philosophy that contrasts sharply with many competitors' safety-focused strategies.

The Revuelto itself represents a significant shift for the Italian manufacturer. As a plug-in hybrid, it blends traditional combustion performance with electric capability, arriving at a moment when even ultra-premium automakers must reconcile performance ambitions with environmental regulations. The car's namesake references a legendary Spanish fighting bull from the Barcelona arena of the 1880s, reflecting Lamborghini's tradition of naming models after celebrated bulls.

Lamborghini's philosophy for the Revuelto and its new SV variant emphasizes creating a visceral connection between driver and machine. Rather than isolating the driver through layers of technology designed to minimize engagement, the brand appears intent on heightening sensory feedback and control. This approach reflects a broader premium positioning: the idea that true luxury in a supercar means feeling every nuance of the driving experience rather than being shielded from it.

The introduction of the SV trim suggests Lamborghini is building out the Revuelto's model range, likely offering enhanced performance specifications, refined handling characteristics, or exclusive features for buyers seeking the pinnacle of what the platform can deliver. Such variants have long been part of Lamborghini's strategy for extending model lifecycles and capturing different segments of its ultra-wealthy customer base.

As the automotive industry continues its transition toward electrification and hybrid powertrains, Lamborghini's approach with the Revuelto demonstrates how legacy supercar manufacturers are attempting to preserve the emotional and sensory rewards of driving while meeting modern regulatory requirements. The SV trim's launch underscores the company's confidence in the hybrid platform as a foundation for future performance innovation.

title: Samsung has new Galaxy headphones in the works
summary: Strings of code in Samsung's Galaxy Wearable app hint at an upcoming pair of over-ear headphones that could compete with the AirPods Max, SamMobile reports. Samsung's reportedly referring to the headphones as the "Galaxy H1," and SamMobile says they could launch sometime in…
whatHappening: Samsung is developing a new pair of over-ear headphones called the Galaxy H1, according to code discovered in its Galaxy Wearable app. The device is positioned as a competitor to Apple's premium AirPods Max.
whoInvolved: Samsung, the South Korean multinational conglomerate and world's fifth-highest valued brand, is building the headphones. Apple's AirPods Max, released in December 2020 as the company's highest-end audio option, serve as the market reference point.
whyMatters: This signals Samsung's push deeper into premium audio hardware, a category dominated by Apple in the high-end segment. If launched, the Galaxy H1 could reshape competitive dynamics in the over-ear wireless headphones market and give Samsung users a flagship audio accessory tightly integrated with their ecosystem.
articleBody:
Samsung appears to be preparing a challenge to Apple's premium headphone offerings. Code found within Samsung's Galaxy Wearable app references an upcoming device called the Galaxy H1, suggesting the company is developing over-ear headphones designed to compete with Apple's AirPods Max. SamMobile reports that the discovery hints at a potential launch sometime in the near future, though Samsung has not yet made any official announcements.

The move represents Samsung's expansion into higher-end audio hardware. While Samsung has offered various earbuds and audio accessories under the Galaxy brand, purpose-built over-ear headphones at a premium tier would mark a more aggressive positioning in the segment currently dominated by Apple. AirPods Max, which launched in December 2020, are Apple's highest-end audio product, sitting at the top of a lineup that includes the base AirPods and the mid-range AirPods Pro.

Samsung's timing and strategy suggest an attempt to capture consumers who own Samsung devices and may currently purchase Apple's premium headphones due to ecosystem integration and lack of comparable alternatives. By developing hardware explicitly named for its Galaxy product family, Samsung is signaling that the H1 is intended as a cornerstone device for users already committed to its smartphone and wearables ecosystem.

The discovery of the Galaxy H1 in app code is a common harbinger of upcoming consumer electronics launches, allowing researchers and tech outlets to identify product plans before manufacturers are ready for public disclosure. The presence of references in the Galaxy Wearable app—software that manages Samsung's connected devices—suggests the headphones are designed to work seamlessly with Samsung phones, tablets, and watches.

Without official specifications or a confirmed launch window, details remain sparse. The internal naming suggests Samsung may eventually market the headphones under a simpler commercial name, though the H1 designation could carry through to the final product. For now, the discovery indicates that Samsung is actively investing in premium audio hardware as part of its broader strategy to compete across consumer electronics categories where Apple has established strong market positions.

title: 2025 GOTY Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is down to $33
summary: For RPG fans who dig Persona-style turn-based action and who are pursuing games with original stories and fantastic tunes, look no further than Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. This praise might come off sounding weird, but I really like that Sandfall Interactive’s breakout hit…
whatHappening: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, a 2025 RPG that has garnered year-end acclaim, is currently discounted to $33. The Verge highlights the game as a standout title for fans of turn-based combat and original narratives.
whoInvolved: Sandfall Interactive developed Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, a dark fantasy RPG published by Kepler Interactive. The Verge, a major technology and culture publication, is covering the game's current promotional pricing.
whyMatters: The sale brings an acclaimed indie RPG to a more accessible price point during the post-holiday season, potentially expanding its audience. For players seeking story-driven alternatives to mainstream franchises, this discount timing could drive meaningful engagement with a game that has already earned recognition as one of 2025's standout releases.
articleBody:
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, one of 2025's most talked-about role-playing games, is now available at a striking discount: $33. The price point, which mirrors the game's own numerical title, represents a significant reduction for a newly released AAA-adjacent title and comes as the game continues to garner critical praise from players and reviewers alike.

Developed by Sandfall Interactive and published by Kepler Interactive, the game has resonated strongly with RPG enthusiasts, particularly those who appreciate Persona-style turn-based action systems. According to The Verge, the title distinguishes itself through its original storytelling and distinctive soundtrack, elements that have become increasingly valuable to a gaming audience fatigued by formulaic experiences. The dark fantasy setting draws from Belle Époque aesthetics, creating a visual and thematic identity that sets it apart from genre contemporaries.

The game follows the members of Expedition 33 as they undertake a perilous journey to destroy the Paintress, a mysterious being responsible for the Gommage—a yearly phenomenon that erases those who have reached or exceeded a progressively lowering age threshold. Players control a party of characters from a third-person perspective, exploring environments and engaging in strategic combat encounters that blend real-time and turn-based elements. This narrative premise—centered on the existential horror of age-based erasure—provides thematic weight that elevates the experience beyond typical dungeon-crawling fare.

The timing of this discount suggests either a planned promotional campaign or publisher confidence in the game's staying power beyond its launch window. For RPG fans still evaluating their 2025 purchases or those who missed the initial release window, the $33 price removes a significant barrier to entry. The game's reception among players who value character-driven storytelling and musical composition indicates that the discount targets an audience already predisposed to appreciate what Sandfall Interactive has created.

title: Trump declares 100 percent tariffs on many drones and all aircraft parts
summary: The United States has already banned future foreign drones from entering the United States unless their companies kiss the ring - as well as routers, robots, and Roombas. Now, President Donald Trump is targeting existing drone imports and parts, too. He's going to try to make…
whatHappening: President Donald Trump is imposing 100 percent tariffs on imported drones and all aircraft parts, escalating trade restrictions on drone and aviation equipment. This move targets both new foreign drone imports and existing supply chains for aircraft components.
whoInvolved: President Donald Trump, the 47th president of the United States and a Republican who previously served as the 45th president from 2017 to 2021, is directing this tariff policy. The action affects foreign drone manufacturers and aircraft parts suppliers seeking to enter the U.S. market.
whyMatters: The tariffs represent a significant expansion of Trump's earlier ban on future foreign drone imports, now targeting existing import flows and critical aviation supply chains. Such protectionist measures could reshape domestic drone and aircraft manufacturing but may also increase costs for businesses relying on these components and trigger retaliatory trade actions.
articleBody:
President Donald Trump is significantly escalating his tariff campaign against foreign technology and manufacturing sectors by imposing 100 percent import duties on drones and all aircraft parts, according to The Verge. The new tariff represents an expansion of earlier restrictions that already prohibited future foreign drone companies from entering the U.S. market unless they comply with stringent government requirements, alongside bans on routers, robots, and robotic vacuums like Roombas.

The tariff structure targets both the importation of completed foreign drones and the component supply chains that feed domestic aircraft manufacturing. By levying a 100 percent duty—effectively doubling the price of these imports—the administration aims to make foreign products economically uncompetitive while incentivizing domestic production and assembly.

A tariff, defined as an import tax imposed by a national government on goods entering its territory and paid by the importer, can serve dual purposes: generating government revenue and regulating foreign trade to protect or encourage domestic industry. Protective tariffs like these are tools designed to burden foreign products and safeguard domestic manufacturers from international competition.

The drone sector has become a particular focus of Trump's trade policy, reflecting broader concerns about foreign technological dominance and supply chain vulnerability in defense-related sectors. The earlier restrictions on future drone imports already created a de facto requirement that foreign companies seeking market access establish American operations or partnerships, fundamentally reshaping the competitive landscape.

These tariffs carry significant implications for aviation manufacturers, defense contractors, and technology companies that depend on imported components. Higher costs for aircraft parts could ripple through the aviation industry and increase expenses for commercial and military aircraft production, while the drone tariffs may accelerate domestic manufacturing investment but at the cost of higher prices for consumers and businesses relying on drone technology.

title: ‘That is not acceptable’: Judge orders Google to make rival app store installs easier
summary: One month after Epic Games and Google seemingly stopped fighting over the future of Android app distribution, they were back in a San Francisco courtroom today - where Judge James Donato just ordered Google to make it easier to install rival app stores on Android. It's been…
whatHappening: A federal judge has ordered Google to make it simpler for Android users to install rival app stores, marking a new development in the ongoing legal battle between Google and Epic Games. Judge James Donato ruled that Google's current practices are unacceptable, forcing the tech giant to lower barriers to alternative app distribution on its platform.
whoInvolved: Epic Games, an American video game and software developer founded in 1991 and now based in Cary, North Carolina, is challenging Google's control over Android app distribution. Google operates Google Play, the official app store for Android devices and a digital distribution service that has dominated mobile app delivery since its inception as the Android Market.
whyMatters: This ruling could fundamentally reshape how Android users access apps, potentially breaking Google's monopoly over app distribution on its own operating system. The decision signals judicial willingness to enforce competition in mobile platforms and could embolden other developers to challenge entrenched app store practices, with implications extending beyond Google to the broader mobile ecosystem.
articleBody:
Judge James Donato's courtroom ruling in San Francisco represents a significant victory for Epic Games in its protracted legal war with Google over Android app distribution. According to The Verge, the judge declared that Google's current approach to rival app stores is "not acceptable," ordering the company to implement measures that would make it substantially easier for users to install competing app stores on their devices. This decision comes just one month after the two companies appeared to have reached some form of settlement, only to return to court for continued litigation.

Google Play has long served as the dominant digital distribution platform for Android applications. The service, which evolved from the original Android Market, remains the primary means through which users discover, download, and install apps on Android devices. Google's control over this distribution channel has been a central point of contention, with Epic Games arguing that the company unfairly leverages its operating system ownership to maintain an anti-competitive stranglehold on app delivery.

The specifics of Judge Donato's order require Google to reduce the friction involved in installing alternative app stores, though the exact technical implementations remain to be determined. This ruling effectively acknowledges that Google's existing barriers—whether technical, contractual, or user-interface-based—constitute an unreasonable impediment to competition. The judge's characterization of the status quo as "not acceptable" suggests a firm judicial stance against Google's current distribution practices.

Epic Games has been waging this fight across multiple fronts. Founded by Tim Sweeney in 1991, the company has grown into a major software publisher with significant industry influence. The company's challenge to Google mirrors its earlier antitrust litigation against Apple, reflecting a broader strategic effort to disrupt app store ecosystems and establish alternative distribution channels that would reduce the commissions extracted by platform holders.

The implications of this ruling extend beyond the immediate parties involved. A successful mandate for easier rival app store installation could fundamentally alter how users access Android applications, potentially fragmenting the app ecosystem while also enabling developers to avoid the commissions that Google currently extracts through Google Play. Other companies and developers may now feel emboldened to pursue similar challenges, knowing that courts are willing to intervene against what they perceive as anti-competitive app store gatekeeping.

title: Apple and Epic argue over how much Apple should get from purchases made outside the App Store
summary: In a new filing in its long-running legal dispute with Epic Games, Apple has proposed a structure that would allow it to collect fees on digital purchases made via external links that don't use the company's in-app purchase system. Epic has already responded, saying that Apple's…
whatHappening: Apple has filed a new proposal in its ongoing legal battle with Epic Games that would allow Apple to collect fees on digital purchases made through external links outside the App Store. Epic Games has already pushed back against the proposal, setting up another round of argument over how much control and revenue Apple should retain from off-platform transactions.
whoInvolved: Apple Inc., the Cupertino-based technology giant founded in 1976 by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak, and Epic Games, a Cary, North Carolina-based video game and software developer founded by Tim Sweeney in 1991, are the primary parties. The two companies have been engaged in a protracted legal dispute over app store policies and revenue sharing.
whyMatters: The outcome of this dispute could fundamentally reshape how app developers and platforms split revenue from digital sales and determine the extent to which Apple can monetize transactions that occur outside its controlled ecosystem. The case has implications for app store economics industry-wide and could set precedent for how much leverage platform companies can exert over developer commerce.
articleBody:
Apple and Epic Games are locked in another critical phase of their long-running legal dispute, this time over how much revenue Apple should extract from digital purchases that bypass its App Store system entirely. According to The Verge, Apple has proposed a fee structure that would allow the company to collect payments on transactions made via external links that don't use Apple's proprietary in-app purchase system. Epic Games has already filed a response rejecting the proposal, signaling that the two companies remain far apart on fundamental questions of platform economics and control.

The dispute centers on a core tension in modern app marketplaces: whether platform owners should be able to profit from transactions that occur through alternative payment channels. Apple has long maintained that its 15 to 30 percent commission on in-app purchases is justified by the value it provides through app discovery, payment processing, and platform security. The company's latest filing suggests it wants to extend its fee collection beyond its walled garden, capturing revenue even when developers direct users to external payment methods.

Epic Games, founded in 1991 by Tim Sweeney and headquartered in North Carolina, has positioned itself as a challenger to Apple's control over app distribution and monetization. The video game and software developer built its reputation on titles like Fortnite, which generated substantial revenue through in-app purchases before becoming a flashpoint in the Apple conflict. Epic's resistance to Apple's latest proposal reflects its broader strategy of arguing that developers should have greater freedom to conduct commerce outside Apple's ecosystem without incurring additional fees.

The legal back-and-forth between these two major technology players represents a fundamental question about platform power in the digital economy. Apple, a multinational technology company headquartered in Silicon Valley since its 1976 founding, has built its business model on controlling the user experience across hardware and software. Epic's challenge to that model, now playing out in court filings and legal arguments, could reshape how the company can monetize its role as gatekeeper to hundreds of millions of devices.

The proposal and Epic's response mark another escalation in what has already become one of the most significant technology industry legal disputes in years. The case touches on issues of antitrust, fair competition, and the proper balance of power between dominant platforms and the developers who build on them. As the two companies continue to argue over fees and control, the outcome could influence how app stores operate globally and determine whether companies like Epic can sustainably challenge Apple's economic dominance.

title: This is Instagram’s new logo
summary: It’s certainly…different. | Image: Meta Instagram has unveiled a new wordmark, moving away from the recognizable cursive typeface it's used over the last decade. The updated wordmark is a strange mix of half-cursive half-print that's somehow less legible than its predecessor.…
whatHappening: Instagram has unveiled a new wordmark logo, replacing the distinctive cursive typeface that defined the platform for over a decade. The redesigned logo blends half-cursive and half-print letterforms in a move that has drawn criticism for reduced legibility.
whoInvolved: Meta Platforms, the multinational technology company headquartered in Menlo Park, California, owns and operates Instagram. Meta's portfolio includes Facebook, WhatsApp, Messenger, and Threads, with advertising accounting for 97.8 percent of the company's revenue as of 2023.
whyMatters: Logo redesigns are high-stakes exercises for social platforms with billions of users and instantly recognizable visual identities. A less legible wordmark could complicate brand recognition across Instagram's ecosystem of features—photo sharing, short-form video, hashtags, and location-based discovery—all elements that depend on clear, intuitive design for user engagement.
articleBody:
Instagram, the photo and short-form video sharing platform owned by Meta Platforms, has introduced a new logo, marking a significant departure from the cursive typeface that has represented the service for the past decade. According to The Verge, the updated wordmark represents a hybrid approach, combining half-cursive and half-print letterforms in a design that critics argue is less legible than its predecessor.

The change reflects a broader evolution in Meta's visual identity strategy across its portfolio of social media properties. Instagram allows users to upload and edit media with filters, organize content through hashtags, and tag locations. The platform's social networking features—including the ability to browse trending content, like posts, and follow other users—have made it a central hub for visual communication worldwide.

The redesign appears counterintuitive given Instagram's existing brand equity. For over a decade, the cursive wordmark became synonymous with the platform, appearing consistently across the app interface, website, advertising materials, and user-generated content. Visual consistency at this scale typically enhances rather than complicates recognition, yet Meta has opted for a typeface that blends letterform styles in ways that may reduce immediate legibility at smaller sizes and across different applications.

The move raises practical questions about implementation. Instagram's wordmark appears in countless contexts—profile headers, notifications, marketing materials, and across Meta's interconnected ecosystem of Facebook, WhatsApp, Messenger, and Threads. A less legible design could fragment how the platform presents itself to its users and the broader public.

Meta's decision to redesign comes amid the company's broader rebranding efforts following its pivot toward metaverse investments and the Threads social media launch. Whether this particular wordmark redesign strengthens or weakens Instagram's position as a dominant visual communication platform remains to be seen, but the immediate reception suggests the design choice may prioritize aesthetic innovation over practical communication clarity.

title: Cats and dogs are missing meals after a popular smart feeder went down
summary: Petlibro’s Granary 2 feeder. | Image: Petlibro A Petlibro outage is preventing its smart pet feeders and other devices from performing scheduled tasks, like dispensing food. The outage began on Tuesday, with users across Reddit reporting that their smart feeders, litter boxes,…
whatHappening: Petlibro's smart pet feeding system has gone offline, leaving pet owners unable to dispense scheduled meals to their cats and dogs. The outage began Tuesday and has affected multiple Petlibro devices, including smart feeders and litter boxes, according to reports from frustrated users.
whoInvolved: Petlibro is a company that manufactures connected pet care devices, including the Granary 2 smart feeder and other IoT-enabled pet products. The outage has impacted pet owners who rely on these devices for automated feeding and pet care management.
whyMatters: The outage exposes the vulnerability of pet care infrastructure that depends on cloud connectivity and company servers. When these systems fail, animals may miss scheduled meals, raising questions about backup mechanisms and the risks of outsourcing critical pet care functions to connected devices.
articleBody:
Petlibro's smart pet feeding ecosystem went offline on Tuesday, disrupting the daily care routines of pet owners who depend on the company's connected devices to dispense meals and manage other tasks. Users across Reddit began reporting that their smart feeders and litter boxes were no longer responding to scheduled commands, leaving their cats and dogs without automatically-dispensed food. The Petlibro Granary 2, one of the company's flagship products, was among the devices affected by the outage.

The outage highlights a growing trend in pet care technology, where connected devices and cloud-based systems handle routine tasks that were once entirely manual. Smart feeders like Petlibro's offerings allow owners to schedule meals, monitor consumption, and control feeding remotely through smartphone apps. These conveniences come with a significant trade-off: when the company's servers go offline, the devices lose core functionality, even if they remain physically present in a pet's home.

According to The Verge, the scope of the outage extends beyond just feeders. Petlibro's product line includes smart litter boxes and other connected pet devices, all of which appear to have been affected when the company's backend systems went down. Pet owners relying on these devices for daily care suddenly had no way to ensure their animals received scheduled meals or had access to clean litter facilities without manual intervention.

For many pet owners, the outage created an urgent practical problem. Those who were at work or away from home when the outage occurred had no way to feed their pets remotely and faced the prospect of animals going hungry until they could manually refill feeders or return home. The incident underscores the dependency that users develop on these systems and the potential consequences when companies providing critical infrastructure experience service disruptions.

The outage raises important questions about device design and fallback mechanisms. Ideally, smart pet feeders would include local backup features that allow scheduled feeding to continue even when cloud connectivity is lost. However, many connected devices prioritize cloud-dependent features over offline functionality, leaving pets vulnerable when internet connectivity or company servers fail.

Petlibro has not yet publicly detailed the cause of the outage or provided a timeline for restoration. As pet owners await service restoration, the incident serves as a reminder of the risks inherent in delegating essential pet care tasks to connected devices that depend on external infrastructure beyond user control.

title: Saber denies replacing Rideshare Stimulator’s writers with ChatGPT

whatHappening: Saber Interactive has denied claims that it replaced writers with ChatGPT on the upcoming Rideshare Stimulator game. The denial comes after former lead writer Stella Sacco publicly stated she was replaced by the AI chatbot.
whoInvolved: Saber Interactive is a video game developer that partnered with Unigine, a company known for its proprietary cross-platform game engine used in simulators and serious games. CEO Matthew Karch represents the company's position, while Stella Sacco, a former lead writer, made the initial replacement claim.
whyMatters: The incident highlights growing tensions in the creative industry over AI integration and job displacement. As studios increasingly explore generative AI tools like ChatGPT, which became widely available in late 2022, questions about whether such technology supplements or replaces human workers will likely intensify across game development and other creative sectors.
articleBody:
Saber Interactive is pushing back against accusations that it replaced human writers with artificial intelligence on an upcoming video game project. CEO Matthew Karch issued a statement denying the allegations, saying, "Neither Saber nor Unigine have replaced any writers with AI," according to The Verge. The dispute centers on the Rideshare Stimulator game, which was announced last month and is being developed by Unigine, the company behind a proprietary cross-platform game engine widely used in simulators and serious games.

The controversy began when Stella Sacco, a former lead writer on the project, claimed publicly that she had been replaced with ChatGPT. Her assertion came amid growing industry adoption of generative AI tools, particularly following ChatGPT's rise to prominence after its release in late 2022. The AI chatbot, developed by OpenAI, uses large language models to generate text in response to user prompts and has become central to broader discussions about artificial intelligence's role in creative work.

Sacco's allegation touches on a concern that has surfaced repeatedly across creative industries in recent months: whether generative AI tools are being used to augment human work or to eliminate jobs outright. Game development, like film, publishing, and other content-creation fields, has faced scrutiny over how studios are integrating AI into their production pipelines. The Rideshare Stimulator project, backed by Unigine's engine technology, became a focal point for this debate.

Karch's categorical denial suggests Saber and Unigine want to distance themselves from the narrative that they have substituted AI for human creative staff. However, the disagreement between company leadership and a former team member indicates deeper questions about how AI tools are being deployed within game development workflows—and whether "replacement" versus "augmentation" represents a meaningful distinction when writing positions are eliminated.

The timing of Sacco's claim is significant, arriving as the industry grapples with how to integrate powerful new technologies responsibly. Studios across the sector continue experimenting with ChatGPT and similar tools for various tasks, from dialogue generation to concept development, even as writers' unions and advocacy groups raise concerns about fair compensation and job security.

title: ‘Zoomsday’ hack uncovered using fewer than 20 AI prompts
summary: Zoom has patched a major security vulnerability that could allow an attacker to hijack anyone's device during a meeting. In a blog post on Tuesday, researchers at A Security say they uncovered the flaw using "fewer than 20 prompts on publicly available AI models," as reported…
whatHappening: Zoom has patched a critical security vulnerability that researchers discovered could allow attackers to hijack devices during video meetings. The flaw was uncovered using fewer than 20 AI prompts on publicly available models, highlighting how AI tools can be weaponized to find security weaknesses.
whoInvolved: Zoom Communications, Inc., the San Jose-based videoconferencing platform company, is the affected party. Security researchers at A Security uncovered the vulnerability and responsibly disclosed it to Zoom before the patch was released.
whyMatters: This vulnerability represents a serious risk to the hundreds of millions of Zoom users worldwide, as device hijacking during meetings could expose sensitive business communications, personal data, and enable further attacks. The discovery method—using AI to efficiently identify security flaws with minimal effort—signals a new threat landscape where vulnerabilities may be discovered and exploited faster than before.
articleBody:
Zoom Communications has moved quickly to patch a major security flaw that researchers say could have allowed attackers to seize control of users' devices during video meetings. The vulnerability, dubbed 'Zoomsday' by security researchers, was uncovered in a striking demonstration of how artificial intelligence tools can be leveraged to find weaknesses in widely used software. According to The Verge, researchers at A Security discovered the flaw using "fewer than 20 prompts on publicly available AI models," suggesting the barrier to finding serious security flaws is rapidly lowering.

Zoom Communications, the American videoconferencing technology company headquartered in San Jose, California, announced the patch on Tuesday through a blog post. The company is primarily known for its Zoom platform, which has become ubiquitous in business, education, and personal communication since its explosive growth during the COVID-19 pandemic. With hundreds of millions of users relying on the platform for daily meetings, a device-hijacking vulnerability poses a substantial risk to both individual privacy and organizational security.

The nature of the flaw suggests it could have had far-reaching consequences if left unpatched. Device hijacking during an active meeting would allow an attacker not only to access sensitive information being discussed but potentially to install malware, access files, or pivot to other systems on a corporate network. The fact that researchers could identify such a critical vulnerability using fewer than 20 AI prompts indicates that the flaw may have been relatively discoverable had a malicious actor applied similar techniques.

The discovery highlights a growing concern in cybersecurity: as artificial intelligence tools become more sophisticated and widely accessible, the ease with which security researchers can find vulnerabilities may be matched—or exceeded—by the ease with which attackers can find them. This compresses the window between discovery and exploitation, making responsible disclosure practices and rapid patching more critical than ever.

Zoom's quick response to patch the vulnerability demonstrates the company's commitment to addressing security issues, but the incident underscores the ongoing challenge of staying ahead of evolving threats. As AI becomes a standard tool in both security research and cyber attacks, companies will need to invest in more advanced threat detection and response capabilities to protect their users.

articleBody:
Bluesky has introduced a targeted feed-filtering feature that addresses one of social media's persistent annoyances: the person who reposts constantly and indiscriminately. Users can now hide reposts from specific accounts without taking the more drastic step of unfollowing them entirely, according to The Verge.

The new tool represents a middle ground between tolerating unwanted content and cutting off an account completely. This is particularly useful for users who want to maintain a connection to someone—whether a friend, colleague, or public figure—but don't want their feed cluttered with that person's reposting habits. The feature appears designed to let users customize their social experience at a granular level.

Bluesky, which is an American microblogging social media service operated by Bluesky Social PBC, has been steadily rolling out quality-of-life improvements as it builds its user base. The platform allows users to share short posts containing text, images, and videos, positioning itself as an alternative to larger established social networks. As the platform matures, features that give users control over their content experience become increasingly central to competitive differentiation.

Feed curation challenges are endemic to social media platforms. Reposts, shares, and retweets can serve legitimate purposes—spreading important information or highlighting valuable content—but can also devolve into noise when individual accounts overuse them. Rather than forcing users into binary choices about whom to follow, Bluesky's selective repost-hiding approach acknowledges the nuance of real social relationships where people want selective connection rather than total inclusion or exclusion.

The feature's rollout suggests Bluesky's product team is focused on practical usability improvements that directly respond to user feedback. As the platform continues to grow, such tools may prove essential in helping users maintain healthy, manageable feeds that reflect their actual interests rather than the posting habits of accounts they're tangentially interested in.

title: Mark Zuckerberg doesn’t understand how to live
summary: Recently, a man I was rock climbing with told me about how he'd used AI to make a motivational poster for himself, which he'd hung on his bedroom wall: a bear, walking a slackline over a canyon, holding a sign that said, "Do cool shit." I made what I hoped was a polite noise.…
whatHappening: The Verge publishes a critical essay questioning Mark Zuckerberg's understanding of how to live a meaningful life. The piece uses a personal anecdote about AI-generated motivational posters as a springboard to examine Zuckerberg's approach to existence and priorities.
whoInvolved: Mark Zuckerberg is the co-founder and CEO of Meta Platforms (formerly Facebook), the world's largest social media company. The Verge is a prominent technology and culture publication covering the intersection of tech, business, and society.
whyMatters: As one of the world's most influential technologists and billionaires, Zuckerberg's worldview shapes decisions affecting billions of users. A critique of his fundamental philosophy about living raises questions about whether the leadership guiding major technology platforms has the wisdom to do so responsibly.
articleBody:
A recent essay in The Verge questions whether Mark Zuckerberg truly understands how to live, using an unexpected cultural moment as its entry point. The piece begins with the author recounting a conversation during a rock climbing outing, where someone mentioned creating an AI-generated motivational poster featuring a bear walking a slackline across a canyon, holding a sign that read, "Do cool shit." The author's polite but pained reaction to this image sets the tone for a larger meditation on contemporary approaches to meaning-making—and by extension, on the tech billionaire who has built his empire by reshaping how billions of people seek, consume, and share experiences.

Zuckerberg, as the co-founder, chairman, CEO, and controlling shareholder of Meta Platforms, wields extraordinary influence over how society communicates and what people pay attention to. His decisions—from algorithm changes to the metaverse pivot to AI investments—touch nearly every corner of modern digital life. Yet according to The Verge, there is a troubling disconnect between Zuckerberg's technical prowess and his grasp of what constitutes a worthwhile life. The AI motivational poster anecdote seems to serve as a symbol of this gap: glossy, generated, optimized for inspirational affect, but fundamentally hollow.

The essay suggests that this misunderstanding may not be merely personal. Zuckerberg's vision for the future—whether through social media platforms designed to maximize engagement or through emerging AI tools that can generate content on demand—reflects a particular philosophy about human flourishing. It is one that privileges novelty, optimization, scalability, and the quantifiable over the organic, the earned, or the deeply considered. A motivational poster made by a machine, no matter how impressive the output, lacks the intentionality and struggle that might make such a thing meaningful.

The Verge does not suggest that Zuckerberg is uniquely confused about life's purpose. Rather, the critique implies that his confusion is consequential precisely because his platforms and technologies are now embedded in the infrastructure of how billions of people navigate existence. If the person shaping those tools fundamentally misunderstands what makes life worth living, that gap compounds across billions of interactions, decisions, and moments of human attention.

What remains at stake is not merely Zuckerberg's personal fulfillment, but whether the systems he has built—and continues to build—are aligned with what humans actually need to flourish. The question of whether a tech CEO understands how to live is, in other words, a question about the future of how everyone else will.

whatHappening: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has published a lengthy manifesto outlining his vision for humanity's future coexistence with artificial intelligence.
